newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: SLOVAK FINMIN SAYS TRADE GAP NO REASON TO DEVALUE.
newsitem.headline: SLOVAK FINMIN SAYS TRADE GAP NO REASON TO DEVALUE.

text.p: Slovak Finance Minister Sergej Kozlik said the country's widening foreign trade deficit in 1996 was no reason to devalue the crown, the pro-government daily Slovenska Republika reported on Monday.
Slovakia posted a foreign trade shortfall of 64.54 billion crowns for the whole of 1996, compared with a revised 5.69 billion crown gap for January-December 1995.
"The deficit itself is no reason to devalue the crown," Kozlik told the paper.
He said the structure of the deficit showed that, with the exception of car imports, there was no significant increase in consumer good imports.
"This factor will not be repeated in 1997 as the temporary lifting of custom duties on car imports with a capacity of up to 1,500 cubic centimetres is no longer valid," he said.
A devaluation of the crown would have a negative impact on imports of techology which Kozlik said Slovakia needs to further boost restructuring of the economy.
"Another reason why we have no need to devalue are stable hard currency reserves," Kozlik said.
Central bank reserves stood at $3.42 billion as of January 29, compared with $3.42 billion a year ago.

Slovakia's current account recorded a deficit for the January-November period of $1.40 billion, compared with a $480.6 million surplus over the same period in 1995, according to figures released on Monday by the National Bank of Slovakia.

Kozlik said the foreign trade balance had also been negatively influenced statistically by a large degree of repayment of foreign receivables in the form of goods, mainly from the former Soviet Union, which are registered as imports.
Last week, the statistical bureau said that such items last year totalled 8.66 billion crowns. A detailed structure of Slovakia's foreign trade balance for 1996 is expected to be released this week.
